title: Arjuna's restless mind
hookLine: between two armies, Arjuna tells Krishna the truth: his mind won't hold still
carry: abhyasa and vairagya: practice and letting go
tomorrow: what did Arjuna see when he aimed at the bird?
last: FIVE TURNINGS, AND EVEN TRUE KNOWING IS ONE TURNINGS, AND EVEN TRUE KNOWING.

lines: THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.
cards: The Bhagavad Gita, chapter six. Two armies wait on the field of Kurukshetra, and in a chariot between them, Krishna has just taught Arjuna how to meditate: sit steady, gather the mind, see the self in all beings.
And Arjuna, the finest archer of his age, says what every beginner thinks. Krishna, I don't see how this can last. The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn.
Holding it is as hard as holding the wind.

teach.h: YES, THE MIND IS LIKE THE WIND.
teach.b: Krishna doesn't argue. Yes, he says, the mind is restless and hard to hold. But by abhyasa, practice, and by vairagya, letting go, it can be held.
Patanjali gives the same pair in sutra 1.12: abhyasa vairagyabhyam tan nirodhah. The turnings are stilled by practice and non-attachment.

teach.h: ABHYASA: THE EFFORT TO STAY STEADY.
teach.b: Practice, 1.13 says, is the effort to stay steady.
And 1.14 adds the fine print: it takes root when it's kept up a long time, without breaks, and with devotion, real care. No shortcut is offered.
Vairagya, in 1.15, is the mastery of someone who no longer thirsts for things, whether seen or only heard about. Commentators take the second to include rewards promised in scripture, even heaven.
So letting go isn't only letting go of dessert. It's letting go of spiritual prizes too. The two balance.
Practice without letting go turns grim and grabby; letting go without practice becomes drift. This is how Hindus have kept a spiritual life for centuries: a practice kept for years, not weeks.
A grandmother's morning puja. A mala of a hundred and eight beads, turned every day. Prayers at dawn, said whether or not anything seems to happen.

That's abhyasa. Doing it without bargaining for results is vairagya, close to what Krishna elsewhere calls acting without clinging to the fruit. Arjuna's honest complaint gets a Hindu answer: not a trick, but two wings.

how: Hindu teachers in yoga and Vedanta lineages describe abhyasa and vairagya as the two wings of spiritual life, practiced through daily meditation or prayer kept up over years and a steady loosening of craving.

o: stilling, holding the mind's turnings still
forcing every thought out by willpower
a blockage of the breath in the body

p: practice: the effort to stay steady

s: non-attachment in 1.15 covers only worldly pleasures
it includes things 'heard about', which commentators take to include heavenly rewards.
sutra 1.14 says practice takes root over a long time, without breaks
the Bhagavad Gita also names practice and detachment for steadying the mind
Krishna's answer to Arjuna in chapter six.

games.q: Nani has turned her mala every morning for fifty years, and says 'nothing special happens.' by Krishna and Patanjali, what is she doing?
o: abhyasa and vairagya: long, unbroken practice, without bargaining for results.
only keeping a family habit, with no teaching behind it.
games.why: long, without breaks, with care: that's abhyasa. no thirst, even for spiritual prizes: that's vairagya. 'nothing special' may be the letting go talking.

practice: If you have a mala or any string of beads, use it: one bead for each soft repetition of a name of God, or of om. If you don't pray, count breaths on your fingers instead. That's practice.
For the second half, keep going, but let go of wanting the sit to go well, wanting calm, wanting insight. Just return, bead by bead, and want nothing from returning.

wordCard.voice: Nirodha, stilling. Abhyasa and vairagya, practice and non-attachment, are what still the mind's turnings: the steady effort to return, and the letting go of thirst.

orig.note: Sanskrit vairāgya: non-attachment, dispassion; literally 'without coloring', from rāga, passion.

carryVoice: Your line: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go. Krishna's answer to the wind. Day four hundred thirty-three, done.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.12–1.16 (practice and non-attachment)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.15 (things heard of: heaven and other promised rewards)
